# Introduction

The permeability coefficient of human skin, $K_p$, is widely used to characterize the rate at which a solute crosses the epidermal barrier and is therefore relevant to transdermal drug delivery, topical formulation, toxicological exposure assessment, and chemical screening. Quantitative structure--permeability relationship (QSPR) models have traditionally treated $K_p$ primarily as a function of molecular properties. The classical Potts--Guy model, for example, related permeability to molecular size and octanol--water partitioning and established a simple physicochemical basis for predicting percutaneous transport [@potts1992]. This view has supported several decades of QSPR development, but it also encourages a convenient simplification: that a reported permeability coefficient can be treated as an observed property of the compound itself.

Literature-derived permeability data challenge that simplification. Measurements collected across studies are generated under different experimental conditions and may differ in temperature, membrane preparation, skin thickness, donor and receptor conditions, analytical procedures, and other protocol-specific factors. Consequently, two measurements for the same compound need not represent repeated observations of a single fixed quantity. Variation between reported values may contain both genuine compound-level permeability signal and systematic experimental or study-level variation. This distinction matters when heterogeneous literature measurements are pooled for QSPR development because the response being modeled is then a mixture of molecular and experimental effects rather than a purely compound-intrinsic endpoint.

The problem of interstudy heterogeneity in skin permeability has been recognized for more than two decades. Fujiwara, Yamashita, and Hashida proposed a *latent membrane permeability* framework in which multiple literature datasets were analyzed simultaneously under the assumption that they shared a common underlying structure--permeability relationship despite differences in absolute permeability among datasets [@fujiwara2003]. Their analysis of ten human and animal skin datasets demonstrated that a common molecular relationship based on lipophilicity and molecular weight could be recovered in the presence of interstudy variability. This work established an important conceptual point: differences among permeability datasets do not necessarily imply different underlying molecular determinants, and study-specific variation can in principle be separated from a shared permeability relationship.

A complementary line of work addressed heterogeneity by standardizing or explicitly modeling experimental conditions. Abraham and Martins adjusted literature human-skin permeability coefficients for ionization and temperature before developing a linear free-energy relationship for permeability at 37 $^\circ$C [@abraham2004]. This approach recognized that literature values measured under different conditions should not necessarily be treated as directly comparable observations. Later, Samaras, Riviere, and Ghafourian analyzed 536 human skin flux reports and incorporated permeant properties, vehicle properties, and experimental factors such as membrane thickness, finite versus infinite dosing, prehydration, and occlusion directly into predictive models [@samaras2012]. Together, these studies show that both study-to-study heterogeneity and measurable experimental conditions can materially affect apparent skin permeation.

The recent database of Cheruvu and colleagues creates an opportunity to revisit these ideas with a data structure that is particularly suitable for hierarchical analysis [@cheruvu2022]. The database contains 476 records for 145 drugs, chemicals, and xenobiotics tested using in vitro human epidermal membranes under aqueous exposure conditions. In addition to permeability coefficients, it records physicochemical descriptors and experimental variables including temperature and skin thickness, while retaining the literature reference from which each measurement was obtained. Because the database contains multiple observations for a number of compounds across a collection of literature sources, the observed response can be represented at its natural measurement level rather than immediately collapsing repeated observations into a single compound mean.

This structure suggests a different formulation of the skin-permeability modeling problem. Instead of assuming that each reported $\log K_p$ value is an error-prone observation of the same compound property, the measurements can be decomposed into a compound-level permeability component, systematic study-level variation, measured experimental-condition effects, and residual experiment-to-experiment variability. For compound $i$ measured in study $j$, we consider the hierarchical representation

$$
\log K_{p,ij}
=
\theta_i
+
u_j
+\beta_T T_{ij}
+\beta_H H_{ij}
+\epsilon_{ij},
$$

where $\theta_i$ represents the compound-level permeability component, $\nu_j$ is a study- or reference-level effect, $T_{ij}$ and $H_{ij}$ represent experimental temperature and skin thickness, respectively, and $\epsilon_{ij}$ represents remaining measurement-level variation. Under this formulation, the quantity of interest for molecular modeling is not necessarily the raw literature measurement but the compound-level permeability after accounting for identifiable experimental and study effects.

The objective of the present study is therefore to determine whether heterogeneous human skin-permeability measurements can be separated into interpretable compound, study, experimental-condition, and residual components, and whether doing so provides a better-defined target for QSPR analysis. We first quantify the relative contributions of compound identity, literature reference, temperature, skin thickness, and residual variation to reported $\log K_p$. We then estimate context-standardized compound-level permeability and examine its relationship with molecular descriptors. Finally, we evaluate whether a hierarchical QSPR, in which molecular effects are estimated while study and experimental heterogeneity are modeled explicitly, provides a more coherent representation of literature-derived permeability data than conventional analysis of raw $\log K_p$ observations. The aim is not to introduce another high-complexity prediction algorithm, but to reconsider what quantity a literature-based skin-permeability QSPR is actually estimating when measurements from heterogeneous experimental sources are pooled.
